title: Developers and Generative AI: A Study of Self-Admitted Usage in Open Source Projects
extended_summary:
This paper investigates how developers self-admit the use of generative AI tools in open-source software development, focusing on ChatGPT and GitHub Copilot. The central question is what software-related tasks developers document as being supported by these LLM-based assistants, and whether the tools were perceived as useful in those contexts. The motivation is to better understand real-world usage patterns, provenance, and traceability of AI-assisted software artifacts.

The study mined GitHub commits, issues, and pull requests containing references to ChatGPT or Copilot, then manually inspected a stratified sample of 1,161 candidate instances. After filtering false positives, the authors analyzed 343 ChatGPT cases and 281 Copilot cases and performed qualitative coding to derive taxonomies of usage tasks. The analysis covered open-source projects hosted on GitHub and included both automatically classifiable Copilot template cases and manually coded instances. No educational intervention, student sample, or achievement outcome is involved.

The paper concludes that developers use generative AI across a broad range of software engineering activities, including feature implementation, process automation, learning, data generation/manipulation, development environment support, software quality, and documentation. ChatGPT was used for a wider and more diverse set of tasks, while Copilot was more concentrated in IDE-integrated workflows such as commit/message generation and development-environment support. The authors argue that these self-admitted traces provide a biased but useful view into LLM adoption in practice, and that future research should better capture AI involvement and evaluate its effects on productivity, code ownership, and quality.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed qualitative mining study with manual coding and taxonomy construction, but it is not an experimental or causal design. The evidence is useful for mapping real-world usage patterns, yet it has clear observational bias and no randomized comparison.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper’s impact is mainly descriptive and methodological rather than demonstrably outcome-changing. It shows broad adoption of LLMs in development workflows, but reports no measured educational effect sizes or direct impact on student achievement.

interventions.use_case: Self-admitted use of ChatGPT to support software-development tasks in open-source projects, including code generation, debugging, refactoring, documentation drafting, brainstorming, and CI/CD assistance.
Self-admitted use of GitHub Copilot for IDE-integrated assistance on development tasks such as commit/PR description generation, code completion, and workflow/script generation.

finding.finding_summary: This qualitative mining study does not estimate a causal effect, but it shows that developers frequently used ChatGPT and Copilot to automate or speed up work such as feature implementation, bug fixing, documentation, and CI/CD scripting. The paper identified 624 valid instances (343 ChatGPT, 281 Copilot) and reports that many task categories were judged useful, especially process automation (21/21 successful for ChatGPT) and several feature- and quality-related tasks.
finding.measure: Self-admitted usage instances and developer-reported usefulness across GitHub commits, issues, and pull requests
finding.study_size: n=624 valid instances (ChatGPT n=343; Copilot n=281)

finding.finding_summary: The paper documents LLM use for brainstorming, program comprehension, and design decisions, suggesting support for problem solving and metacognitive work rather than direct instruction. At the same time, it highlights limitations such as hallucinations and ownership concerns, so the net effect on deeper understanding is mixed and not quantified.
finding.measure: Qualitative coding of learning/brainstorming/comprehension usage in developer artifacts
finding.study_size: n=624 valid instances overall; learning-related instances are a subset (e.g., ChatGPT learning n=64 in the taxonomy)

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that widespread self-admitted AI use raises provenance, code ownership, trust, licensing, and review-process concerns for open-source projects. It reports no quantitative institutional effect, but provides evidence that projects may need new contribution and review guidelines for AI-generated code and that mining studies must adapt to harder-to-detect AI involvement.
finding.measure: Qualitative analysis of governance/provenance implications discussed in developer artifacts and author interpretation
